The most striking thing about this list of opinions on what constitute distorted thinking is the optimism bias. Some examples:

Filtering: You take the negative details and magnify them [...]

Catastrophizing: You expect disaster.

Global Labeling: You generalize one or two qualities (in yourself or others) into a negative global judgment.

Each of these can be made opposite, yet the author(s) chose to focus on pessimism. This already indicates the "helpful advice" of the article is corrupted by the authors own inability to recognize circumstantial reality. Sometimes you are powerless, sometimes you should expect disaster, but of course the charitable view is to assume he means "when unwarranted" (a point carelessly not clarified). Even if that is the case, this particular quote suggests an absence of due diligence in framing these "guidelines":

Shoulds: You have a list of ironclad rules about how you and other people should act.

This describes ethics. Everyone has ideas on morality, what "should" be done is necessary to evaluate if two or more people exist together. The idea one should eschew analyzing morality, or determining morality of actions, is utterly absurd. It is not a "distortion" to evaluate whether an act is good or bad according to your understanding of whether things harm or help others.

Really, the absence of critical thought in this article is ironic for a place supposing to encourage critical thought. It is a very bad list of opinions that is fraught with ambiguity and carelessness.
